title: Death and the Dies irae
subtitle: A funeral chant among bells, bones and piano keys

hero.file: File:The Triumph of Death by Pieter Bruegel the Elder.jpg
hero.caption: Pieter Bruegel the Elder, The Triumph of Death, about 1562. Skeletons overrun a barren landscape.

intro: A single voice leads into funeral bells, rattling bows and thunderous piano chords. The Dies irae passes through Berlioz, Liszt, Saint-Saëns and Rachmaninoff, while Verdi sets its Latin words blazing in the Requiem.

stations.title: A hymn in one voice

art.file: File:The Triumph of Death by Pieter Bruegel the Elder.jpg
art.caption: Bruegel’s The Triumph of Death, about 1562. Death rides a chestnut horse ahead of an army of skeletons.

stations.text:
Gareth Hughes sings Pange lingua alone, letting each Latin phrase rise, turn and settle before the next breath. The Eucharistic hymn’s stanza melody returns with fresh words; the whole performance rests on a single human voice.

At Catholic funerals, the Dies irae supplied a sterner melody. Its first eight notes in the Vatican Graduale are F–E–F–D–E–C–D–D. Berlioz will set that melody deep in his orchestra. In Bruegel’s The Triumph of Death, skeletons have already crossed the landscape, driving the living before them.

cues.text: Gareth Hughes sings Pange lingua, the Latin Eucharistic hymn, in a single unaccompanied line.
Fresh Latin words fill the familiar phrases as the stanza melody returns.
The closing stanzas carry the same melody towards the hymn’s final prayer.

stations.title: Funeral bells at the witches’ sabbath
stations.text:
Bells toll C and G in the finale of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique. His artist is dreaming of his own funeral, surrounded by witches and monsters. Out of the orchestra’s depths comes the Dies irae, its first statement assigned to four bassoons and two ophicleides, the keyed brass instruments in Berlioz’s score.

The chant moves in long, heavy notes. Then the same tune shrinks into quicker phrases and passes to brighter wind and brass voices. In his 1845 programme, Berlioz calls this a ‘burlesque parody’: the funeral music is beginning to dance.

cues.text: Deep bells toll C and G around the approaching funeral chant.
The Dies irae sounds low and broad, scored for four bassoons and two ophicleides.
The chant’s long notes shorten as the melody passes through brighter wind and brass voices.

stations.title: The witches crowd the dance
stations.text:
The witches’ round begins low in the strings, with cellos and double basses setting off together. Violas answer, then violins; each group starts while the earlier players continue. The tune’s quick rise and accented turn keep appearing in different corners of the orchestra, like dancers joining a crowded ring.

Berlioz has saved another encounter for later: the Dies irae will stride through this running dance. For now, the round occupies the foreground, swelling as winds and brass join the strings. Towards the end of this passage, the bustle subsides into held notes, leaving room for quiet horn calls.

cues.text: The string parts overlap, each new entry joining the dance before the earlier one has finished.
Woodwinds, brass and percussion join the strings’ imitative dance.
The rushing dance thins into held notes before the horns call the chant back.

stations.title: Liszt’s piano changes its voice
stations.text:
Liszt’s B-minor Sonata begins with low Gs and a falling scale, leaving silence around each phrase. Then the piano leaps into octaves and hammers a repeated note. A few minutes later, broad D-major chords open out under the marking Grandioso.

Liszt had heard the première of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique in 1830 and transcribed it for piano in 1833. In Totentanz, he built variations for piano and orchestra around the Dies irae. The Sonata’s drama grows from its own terse beginnings: even beneath the broad Grandioso melody, the accompaniment keeps striking repeated quavers.

cues.text: Low Gs and falling scales begin Liszt’s B-minor Sonata, with silence between the phrases.
The piano breaks into leaping octaves, then strikes a repeated note like a hammer.
Broad D-major chords announce the Grandioso; repeated quavers keep sounding beneath the melody.

stations.title: Death’s fiddle and the rattling bows
stations.text:
Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique returns for its final rush. The wind and brass carry the funeral chant in broad notes while the strings race through the witches’ round. Later, violins and violas turn their bows over and strike with the wood: col legno, a dry rattle across the strings.

In Saint-Saëns’s Danse macabre of 1874, Death takes up a solo violin and the xylophone rattles like bones. The woodwinds quote the Dies irae amid the dance. That score grew from a song on Henri Cazalis’s poem; Berlioz’s sabbath ends with the strings bowing again and the full orchestra hammering out C major.

cues.text: Berlioz’s orchestra gathers force after the quiet horn calls, preparing the chant and round together.
Wind and brass carry the broad funeral chant while the strings race through the witches’ dance.
Violins and violas strike their strings with the wood of their bows: col legno, a dry rattle.

stations.title: Verdi’s chorus faces judgement
stations.text:
Four orchestral blows tear into Verdi’s Dies irae; rushing figures drive towards the chorus’s entrance. The ancient Latin words describe the day of judgement, and Verdi gives them a new tune with the force of a shouted warning. This Requiem first sounded in Milan’s church of San Marco on 22 May 1874.

After the uproar, the voices grow quiet on ‘Quantus tremor’ — ‘how great the trembling’. Repeated syllables make the choir sound as though its breath has begun to shake. The orchestra still moves beneath it, while the people who proclaimed the day of wrath tremble at its approach.

cues.text: Four orchestral blows and rushing figures launch Verdi’s setting of the Latin judgement scene.
The orchestra softens, and the chorus’s words begin to stand out against the quieter accompaniment.
‘Quantus tremor’ — ‘how great the trembling’ — breaks into quiet, repeated syllables.

stations.title: Three notes beside a painted boat

art.file: File:Arnold Böcklin - Die Toteninsel I (Basel, Kunstmuseum).jpg
art.caption: Arnold Böcklin, Isle of the Dead, first version, 1880. A white-cloaked figure stands beside a shrouded coffin in the boat.

stations.text:
Rachmaninoff plays his C♯-minor Prelude in this 1919 recording. Three low notes, A–G♯–C♯, ring out; the answering chords are almost whispered. Soon the right hand begins running in triplets, carrying a descending melody inside the restless notes.

Böcklin’s Isle of the Dead places a white-cloaked figure and a coffin in a boat approaching the island. A black-and-white reproduction caught Rachmaninoff’s eye in 1907. His orchestral Isle of the Dead takes up the Dies irae in fragments and longer phrases; at the piano, the Prelude’s triplets gather towards a return of those three bass notes.

cues.text: Rachmaninoff opens his C♯-minor Prelude with A–G♯–C♯ in low octaves, followed by hushed chords.
A descending melody sounds inside the right hand’s running triplets.
The Prelude’s triplets gather force, carrying the piano towards the return of its opening chords.

stations.title: The piano fills the room
stations.text:
The C♯-minor Prelude reaches its great return: the quiet opening chords now spread across four staves, two for each hand, marked fff pesante — very loud and heavy. The three-note call has become a peal of bells.

In the Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini of 1934, Rachmaninoff would give the piano another imposing melody. Variation VII puts the Dies irae in chords against Paganini’s tune in bassoons and plucked cellos. Here the Prelude draws back from its own climax. A low C♯ stays beneath changing chords, until the final C♯-minor chord fades to ppp.

cues.text: Running triplets drive towards the Prelude’s huge return, written on four staves.
A low C♯ anchors the coda while quieter chords settle above it.
